entities.name: Iona Abbey
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Iona Abbey on the Isle of Iona, off the western coast of Scotland, founded by the Irish monk Columba (Colum Cille) in 563 CE, is the founding institution of Celtic Christianity in Scotland and Northumbria — the monastery from which missionaries converted northern Britain, produced the Book of Kells (possibly begun at Iona), and transmitted the insular minuscule script that became medieval Europe's dominant writing hand. Iona's influence over early medieval Britain is disproportionate to its tiny size: a 5.5 km² island whose monastery shaped the religious culture of hundreds of thousands.

Columba, a Irish nobleman and monk who had fled Ireland after a dispute over a psalter (possibly causing the Battle of Cúl Dreimhne, 561 CE), established his monastery on Iona as both penitential exile and missionary base. Iona's scriptorium produced illuminated manuscripts in the insular tradition; monks from Iona founded Lindisfarne (635 CE) on the northeast English coast, which became the greatest center of Northumbrian Christianity and produced the Lindisfarne Gospels. Iona's 'school' of abbots trained missionaries who Christianized the Picts of Scotland.

Viking raids beginning in 795 CE devastated Iona repeatedly — the Martyrdom of 68 monks in 806 CE forced the transfer of many monks and treasures (possibly including the Book of Kells) to Kells in Ireland. The Iona Community — a modern ecumenical Christian community founded in 1938 by George MacLeod — rebuilt the ruined abbey and continues its use as an active center of Christian pilgrimage, social justice advocacy, and community living. Over 250,000 people visit annually.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Iona Abbey — from a 5.5 km² island — transmitted Celtic Christianity to Scotland and Northumbria, possibly produced the Book of Kells, and founded Lindisfarne's scriptorium, making it the most consequential tiny monastery in European history in terms of the territory converted and the manuscripts produced.
